concept.name: Bit Manipulation Techniques

relationships.description: Connects Bit Manipulation Techniques to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Bit manipulation operates directly on binary representations using single-cycle CPU instructions (`AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, shifts, `POPCNT`, `TZCNT`) for compact sets, fast math, and lock-free flags.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use bitmasks and bitwise idioms for compact state flags, power-of-two alignment, and $O(1)$ parity/isolation tricks—while guarding against signed-shift UB and unreadable cleverness.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern CPUs execute bitwise operations and hardware intrinsics (`POPCNT`, `LZCNT`, `TZCNT`) in 1–3 clock cycles with zero branching. Bitsets shrink memory footprints by 8x–64x (fitting Bloom filters, inverted indexes, and permission masks into L1 cache), and power-of-two bitmasks replace expensive modulo instructions in hash tables and ring buffers.
whenToUse: Compact boolean flag sets (UNIX file permissions `0755`, feature flags, TCP header flags `SYN|ACK`).
Power-of-two ring buffers and hash tables (`index & (capacity - 1)` instead of `index % capacity`).
Space-critical membership structures (Bloom filters, Roaring Bitmaps, CPU affinity masks) where 1 bit per item fits in L1/L2 cache.
whenNotToUse: General business logic where named booleans or enums are clearer and performance is I/O-bound.
Dynamic sets with >64 elements unless using a multi-word `BitSet` / Roaring Bitmap library.
Cryptographic or arbitrary-precision arithmetic where timing side-channels or overflow semantics require specialized libraries.
keyPoints: Core single-bit ops on mask `m`: test `(m >> i) & 1`, set `m | (1 << i)`, clear `m & ~(1 << i)`, toggle `m ^ (1 << i)`.
Lowest set bit isolation: `x & -x` extracts the least-significant 1-bit (powering Fenwick / Binary Indexed Trees).
Brian Kernighan's trick: `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit—testing power-of-two via `x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0`.
XOR self-inverse (`a ^ a == 0`, `a ^ 0 == a`): finds the unique non-duplicate element in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space without a hash map.
Hardware bit-count & scan: `int.bit_count()` (Python 3.10+), `Integer.bitCount()` (Java), and `__builtin_popcountll` compile to single `POPCNT` instructions.

examples.title: Lock-Free Ring Buffer Index Wrapping (LMAX Disruptor)
examples.scenario: A high-throughput Java Disruptor queue sizes its ring buffer to `65,536` ($2^{16}$) slots and maps monotonically increasing `long` sequence numbers to array slots.
examples.outcome: Computing `slot = sequence & 65535` takes 1 CPU cycle instead of an integer division (`%`), avoiding signed-negative remainder bugs and sustaining >10M ops/sec.

examples.title: Single-Number & Missing-Number Deduplication
examples.scenario: An embedded diagnostic stream has $N - 1$ paired sensor IDs and one unpaired ID in a read-only 4 KB RAM budget.
examples.outcome: XORing all IDs cancels every pair (`id ^ id == 0`) and leaves the exact unpaired ID in $O(1)$ extra memory.

tradeOffs.pro: Fits in a single CPU register (8 bytes); union (`|`), intersection (`&`), and difference (`& ~`) run in 1 cycle.
tradeOffs.con: Hard-capped at 64 items per word; expanding past 64 requires multi-word arrays or Roaring Bitmaps.

tradeOffs.pro: Avoids 15–40 cycle integer `DIV` instructions and handles wrap-around cleanly.
tradeOffs.con: Forces buffer capacities to double (2x memory jumps) instead of growing by 1.5x or arbitrary primes.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates branch-misprediction penalties (~15 cycles) on unpredictable random inputs.
tradeOffs.con: Obscures intent for maintainers and can inhibit compiler auto-vectorization if overused.

failureModes.name: 32-bit Shift Overflow (`1 << 31` / `1 << k`)
failureModes.description: In C/C++/Java, `1` defaults to a signed 32-bit `int`; shifting `1 << 31` or `1 << 40` triggers undefined behavior (C/C++) or wraps modulo 32 (Java), silently corrupting 64-bit masks.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use typed unsigned/64-bit literals (`1ULL << k` in C++, `1L << k` in Java).

failureModes.name: Operator Precedence Bug (`flags & MASK == MASK`)
failureModes.description: In C, Java, and Python, `==` binds tighter than `&`, `|`, and `^`, so `flags & MASK == MASK` parses as `flags & (MASK == MASK)`.
failureModes.mitigation: Always parenthesize bitwise expressions: `(flags & MASK) == MASK`.

failureModes.name: Signed Right-Shift Sign Extension
failureModes.description: Right-shifting a negative signed integer (`-1 >> 1`) in Java/C++ copies the sign bit (arithmetic shift), leaving 1s at the top.
failureModes.mitigation: Use unsigned types (`uint64_t`) or Java's logical right-shift operator `>>>`.

failureModes.name: Python Arbitrary-Precision Sign Bit Surprise
failureModes.description: In Python, `~x` produces `-(x + 1)` with infinite leading 1s rather than a fixed-width unsigned complement.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly mask widths with `& ((1 << W) - 1)` when emulating fixed-width registers.

commonMistakes: Writing `1 << i` instead of `1L << i` or `1ULL << i` when `i >= 31`.
Omitting parentheses around `(x & mask) != 0`, letting `!=` bind before `&`.
Using `x & (x - 1) == 0` to check power-of-two without guarding `x > 0` (it falsely returns true for `0`).
Using the XOR swap trick (`a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b`) when `a` and `b` can alias the same memory address, zeroing both.
Reimplementing popcount loops manually instead of calling `Integer.bitCount()` or `int.bit_count()`.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every integer in hardware is a fixed-width vector of bits. Instead of treating those bits solely as a base-10 number, bit manipulation treats them as parallel boolean lanes or algebraic elements over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Operations like `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, and bit-shifts act on all 64 lanes simultaneously in a single CPU cycle, enabling $O(1)$ set algebra, alignment to cache-line or page boundaries (`(addr + 4095) & ~4095`), and branchless invariants.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a **Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)** uses `x & -x` (lowest set bit) to update and query prefix sums over an array of size 16 in $O(\log N)$:

1. Suppose index `i = 6` (`0110` in binary) receives `+5`.
2. `i & -i` computes `0110 & 1010 = 0010` (`2`), meaning `tree[6]` covers 2 elements (`[5..6]`).
3. Add `i += (i & -i)` -> `6 + 2 = 8` (`1000`), updating `tree[8]` (covers `[1..8]`), then `8 + 8 = 16` (`10000`), updating `tree[16]`.
4. To query `prefix_sum(7)` (`0111`), subtract `i -= (i & -i)`: `7 -> 6 -> 4 -> 0`, summing `tree[7] + tree[6] + tree[4]` in just 3 array reads.

sections.content:
## Two's complement & page alignment

Two's complement makes `-x == (~x) + 1`, which explains both `x & -x` and fast alignment. To round a memory size `n` up to the next multiple of a power-of-two `align` (such as a 4,096-byte OS page or 64-byte CPU cache line), compute `(n + align - 1) & ~(align - 1)`. This avoids division and guarantees cache-line alignment in allocators and SIMD buffers.

## Essential bit-manipulation idioms

| Operation | Idiom | Notes / Edge case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Test bit `i` | `(x >> i) & 1` | Use `>>>` in Java for signed ints |
| Isolate lowest 1-bit | `x & -x` | Returns `0` when `x == 0` |
| Clear lowest 1-bit | `x & (x - 1)` | Power-of-2 check needs `x > 0` |
| Align up to `2^k` | `(n + A - 1) & ~(A - 1)` | `A` must be a power of 2 |
| Enumerate submasks of `m` | `s = (s - 1) & m` | Visits all $2^{\|m\|}$ submasks in descending order |

## Failure modes

- **Undefined behavior in C/C++**: Shifting by $\ge$ bit-width (`x << 64`) or left-shifting a negative number is UB and allows compilers to misoptimize surrounding checks.
- **32-bit vs 64-bit literal mismatch**: Writing `1 << i` in Java or C++ truncates masks above bit 30.
- **Unmasked Python `~`**: `~0b1010` yields `-11`, not `0b0101`, breaking unsigned equality checks unless masked with `& ((1 << width) - 1)`.

## Submask enumeration idiom

A classic pattern for both bitsets and bitmask DP is iterating over every non-empty subset `sub` of a bitmask `mask`:

`sub = mask; while sub > 0: ...; sub = (sub - 1) & mask`

Each step clears the lowest bit of `sub` and restores any lower bits present in `mask`, visiting all $2^k$ subsets in descending order without recursion or duplicate checks.

## Practical checklist

- Use explicit 64-bit unsigned literals (`1ULL << k`, `1L << k`) for any mask that can exceed 30 bits.
- Parenthesize all `&`, `|`, and `^` subexpressions inside comparisons.
- Prefer standard intrinsics (`int.bit_count()`, `Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros()`) over manual bit loops.
- Guard `x > 0` before applying `x & (x - 1) == 0` for power-of-two checks.
- Document non-obvious bit hacks with the invariant they maintain.

interviewProblems.title: Bit Manipulation Techniques
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Bit Manipulation Techniques. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Bit manipulation operates directly on binary representations using single-cycle CPU instructions (`AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, shifts, `POPCNT`, `TZCNT`) for compact sets, fast math, and lock-free flags.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Clear LSB: x & (x-1) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with CPU Intrinsics.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, CPU Intrinsics experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always use typed unsigned/64-bit literals (`1ULL << k` in C++, `1L << k` in Java).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use bitmasks and bitwise idioms for compact state flags, power-of-two alignment, and $O(1)$ parity/isolation tricks—while guarding against signed-shift UB and unreadable cleverness.
Avoid trap: Writing `1 << i` instead of `1L << i` or `1ULL << i` when `i >= 31`.
Avoid trap: Omitting parentheses around `(x & mask) != 0`, letting `!=` bind before `&`.
When to reach for it: Compact boolean flag sets (UNIX file permissions `0755`, feature flags, TCP header flags `SYN|ACK`).
When to reach for it: Power-of-two ring buffers and hash tables (`index & (capacity - 1)` instead of `index % capacity`).

putItTogether.summary: Use bitmasks and bitwise idioms for compact state flags, power-of-two alignment, and $O(1)$ parity/isolation tricks—while guarding against signed-shift UB and unreadable cleverness.

putItTogether.outcome: Computing `slot = sequence & 65535` takes 1 CPU cycle instead of an integer division (`%`), avoiding signed-negative remainder bugs and sustaining >10M ops/sec.
